title: The feasts, again
tomorrow: 'the glory of God is a person fully alive.' is that what he said?

segments.voice: The Apocalypse ended on all things new: the old, renewed. Today, a renewal that comes around every single year, in color.

A phone calendar runs on months and reminders. Sit in a Catholic church across one whole year and a second calendar shows up, in cloth. Violet in Advent and Lent. White and gold at Christmas and Easter. Green through the long ordinary weeks. Red at Pentecost and on the feasts of martyrs. The priest's vestments change, and so do the cloths on the altar. Why keep changing colors?
screen: `A SECOND CALENDAR, IN CLOTH.` → `VIOLET, WHITE, GREEN, RED.` → `WHY KEEP CHANGING?`

segments.voice: Because the year is telling a story, and the story is Christ's life, told again every year. Advent waits for his coming. Christmas celebrates his birth. Lent walks toward the cross. Easter is the rising, and Pentecost the Spirit. Then the long green stretch called Ordinary Time, the season of growing, ends with the feast of Christ the King, and the year turns over into Advent again. The Church doesn't just tell this story; it lets you smell and touch it. Ashes on the forehead to open Lent. Palm branches in your hand the Sunday before Easter. A new fire lit in the dark at the Easter Vigil. Every season carries its own sense. Ecclesiastes says it in the Douay-Rheims: "All things have their season." Something to tell a friend tonight: the Christmas chants in Latin sing hodie, today. Today Christ is born. Not long ago, today. The feasts don't treat the life of Christ like history to remember. They treat it like something happening again, this year, to you. Even the plain weekdays sit inside a season, so the ordinary days are part of the story too.
screen: `THE YEAR TELLS CHRIST'S LIFE.` · `ADVENT TO CHRIST THE KING.` · `ASHES, PALMS, NEW FIRE.` · `HODIE: TODAY.` · then, large: `THE TURNING YEAR.`

segments.voice: Find one object near you that's green, the color of the Church's ordinary weeks, or violet, white or red if you know the season. Rest your eyes on it, its exact shade and edges. Let it stand for today: one day, held inside a much longer story.
The feasts. The Church's days of celebration, set through a year that turns around the life of Christ.
Here's the line: the turning year, one color and one feast at a time. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics follow the liturgical year from Advent to Christ the King; the Church's calendar gives each day a season, and many days a feast or a saint's memorial, often marked in parish bulletins and missals.

chat.meaning: The liturgical year retells Christ's life from Advent to Christ the King, so even ordinary weeks belong to one turning story.

Advent.meaning: the season of waiting before Christmas

Lent.meaning: the season of prayer and fasting before Easter

Ordinary Time.meaning: the Church's long green season between the big feasts

Christ the King.meaning: the feast that closes the Church's year
